As for the claims therein, the idea that SK or Indo would engage in a currency devaluation battle is flatly idiotic. SK has already signed an agreement to begin free trade with China this fall, and Indonesia's currency is so weak they are struggling to import the advanced technology their economy needs to function properly.

The problem with the devaluation, and I say this as someone who is up to his neck in the export business, is that it came as a total surprise to everyone and has not been supported by any sort of public policy stance to give us an idea of just how far the government is willing to drop the value. Anyone who looks at a 5% devaluation and then immediately cuts their export prices by 5% to increase their competitive advantage is a fool. What happens in 3 weeks or 3 months when the value creeps back up? Do you suffer the loss in margin or piss off your international distributors by changing the prices twice in a row, and the second time in a direction that doesn't help them?
